summary: Defines Trickle ICE, an extension of the ICE protocol for finding a working network path between two endpoints. Instead of gathering every possible address before starting, agents exchange candidates gradually and begin connectivity checks right away. This can speed up setting up a session considerably.

eli5.summary: Imagine searching for the best way to reach a friend's house. Instead of listing every possible route before leaving, you start walking and keep texting new routes as you find them. You arrive sooner.

subtitle: Start testing network paths while addresses are still being discovered, instead of waiting for the full list.

tldr.problem: Regular ICE gathers all candidates, including slow STUN and TURN lookups, before connectivity checks begin, so sessions can take a long time to set up.
tldr.mechanism: Trickle ICE lets agents send candidates one at a time as they are found and start connectivity checks as soon as a candidate pair exists, so gathering and checking run in parallel.
tldr.outcome: Sessions can be established considerably faster. RFC 8838 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8863.

today: RFC 8838 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021 and is updated by RFC 8863. It has not been obsoleted. It defines the generic behavior, while protocol-specific usage such as SIP is in RFC 8840.

sections.title: Why ICE Needed Trickling
sections.content:
The Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) protocol in RFC 8445 has an agent gather candidates (possible addresses), swap them with a peer, pair them up, run connectivity checks, and finally pick the pair to use. Gathering often means asking STUN servers (RFC 5389) and allocating relayed addresses on TURN servers (RFC 5766), which can make session setup slow.

Trickle ICE is a supplementary mode in which candidates are exchanged incrementally as soon as they become available, while other candidates are still being gathered. Checks can start as soon as a pair exists. The RFC also says how to detect support, how the ICE rules change, and how a Trickle ICE agent can work with an ordinary RFC 8445 agent.

The document defines no protocol-specific usage. That is left to usage documents such as RFC 8840 for SIP and SDP, and XEP-0176 for XMPP. The RFC notes the technique has operational history going back to 2005, with the XMPP Jingle 'dribble mode'.
sections.eli5: Normally two computers write down every possible way to reach each other before they try any. Trickle ICE lets them start trying right away and keep adding new ways as they find them.

sections.title: Detecting Support and Starting a Session
sections.content:
A using protocol SHOULD either offer a capabilities discovery method so agents can check for Trickle ICE support before starting, or make support mandatory. If an agent learns the other side lacks support, it MUST fall back to regular ICE or abandon the session.

Without discovery, an agent can put the ICE option trickle in its ICE description. It must be given at the session level or for every data stream, never for only some streams. In SDP, the encoding is defined in RFC 8840.

The initiator may send any mix of candidates in the initial ICE description: all it plans to use, only a publicly reachable one, or none. The responder replies with its own initial ICE response, which also may contain any set of candidates, including none. If the responder sees no Trickle ICE support, it MUST follow regular ICE.
sections.eli5: First each side says 'I can do the fast way'. If the other side cannot, they go back to the slow, careful way.

sections.title: Trickling and Pairing Candidates
sections.content:
When an agent finds a new local candidate, it works out priority, type, foundation and component ID as in regular ICE. If the transport address and base match an existing local candidate, the new one is redundant and ignored, regardless of priority. Otherwise it is trickled to the remote agent through the using protocol.

The using protocol MUST deliver each candidate, and any end-of-candidates indication, exactly once and in the order sent. Trickling must also be tied to a specific ICE session, identified by the Username Fragment and Password combination, so delayed updates from before an ICE restart can be ignored.

An agent MUST NOT pair a local candidate until it has been trickled to the remote party. A pair with a server-reflexive local candidate has that candidate replaced by its base before redundancy tests. Pruning only looks at pairs in the Waiting or Frozen state, so checks already in flight or finished are not disturbed. If a checklist already holds the maximum of 100 pairs (the RFC 8445 default), the agent SHOULD discard Failed pairs first, then lower-priority ones.
sections.eli5: Each new route is only added to your list after you have told your friend about it. That way you both try the same routes at about the same time.

sections.title: Checklists That Grow While Running
sections.content:
A checklist can start empty and be filled as candidates arrive. An empty checklist still starts in the Running state, and a Trickle ICE agent MUST keep each checklist Running as long as it expects pairs to be added. When timer Ta fires and an empty checklist is picked, nothing happens and the agent moves straight to the next Running checklist.

Regular ICE marks a checklist Failed when all pairs have Failed or Succeeded and no valid pair exists for each component. With trickling that would often fire too early, so two more conditions apply: all local gathering has completed, and the remote agent has sent an end-of-candidates indication for that checklist.

A newly formed pair gets its starting state from three rules. If it is the topmost pair for its foundation, it is set to Waiting. If at least one pair for that foundation has Succeeded, it is Waiting. In all other cases it is Frozen.
sections.eli5: Your to-do list can start empty. You do not give up just because the list looks empty right now, because new items are still coming in.

sections.title: End-of-Candidates and ICE Restarts
sections.content:
When gathering for a data stream is complete or has expired, the agent sends an end-of-candidates indication, which MUST name the generation (Username Fragment and Password). It can ride in the initial request, with the last candidate, or stand alone. After sending it, an agent MUST NOT convey any more candidates, and a receiver MUST ignore any candidates that arrive afterwards for that stream.

A controlled agent SHOULD send it once gathering for a stream is done. A controlling agent MAY finish ICE before sending all of them, but sending them is RECOMMENDED. Receiving one lets an agent mark checklists Failed sooner, or stop waiting for better candidates when it already has a working pair on a lower-preference transport such as TURN.

Nothing here changes how ICE concludes: nomination still happens, and no new candidates may be trickled after a pair is nominated. Adding candidates later needs an ICE restart. If Trickle ICE support was already established, it can be assumed to still apply after a restart.
sections.eli5: When you have run out of new routes, you tell your friend 'that is all of them'. After that, nobody adds more.

sections.title: Half Trickle and Old Peers
sections.content:
In half trickle, the initiator gathers a full generation of candidates before sending the initial ICE description, which still indicates Trickle ICE support. A regular ICE responder can process it, while a Trickle ICE responder can answer with fewer candidates and trickle the rest. It is meant for cases where support cannot be confirmed in advance, and gives roughly half the benefit. An end-of-candidates indication is optional in it, since the initiator may still trickle later.

Half trickle is only needed for the first exchange. Afterwards both sides know whether Trickle ICE is supported. If gathering starts early, on cues such as keypad activity or the phone going off hook, half trickle can approach the speed of full trickle.

Appendix A explains why plain ICE cannot simply be used: for example, a lone candidate that happens to hit an unrelated host can produce a Failed pair and an empty valid list, failing ICE too early. Appendix B notes that an ICE-lite agent needs no special rules, and a full agent may skip trickling when it learns the peer is ICE-lite.
sections.eli5: If you are not sure your friend knows the fast way, you first send a short list of routes they can read the old way, and keep texting new ones if it turns out they can handle it.

sections.title: Requirements for Using Protocols and Security
sections.content:
Section 18 lists what a using protocol must provide. It SHOULD let parties advertise and discover support before a session. It MUST offer a way to trickle candidates after the initial description, deliver each candidate or end-of-candidates indication exactly once and in order, let both parties agree on the ICE session in force, and carry the end-of-candidates indication naming that session.

For IANA, the RFC registers the ICE option trickle, meaning support for incremental communication of ICE candidates.

On security, Trickle ICE inherits the considerations of RFC 8445. If revealing host addresses is a privacy concern, an agent can send descriptions with no candidates and trickle only candidates that do not reveal host addresses, such as relayed ones. The RFC refers to RFC 8828 for related discussion.
sections.eli5: The messenger service you use to send routes has to deliver every message once and in order. If you do not want to reveal your home address, you can share only addresses of a helper in the middle.
